label: Blue Note
rationale: Sonny Clark's final album as leader and, in AllMusic's words, 'a definitive recording for Clark, and really for all time in the mainstream jazz idiom' (S1, Michael Nastos, four-and-a-half stars). It is the strongest single case for Clark's own compositional voice — he wrote four of the six originals — and the hard-bop quintet writing here ('Somethin' Special', 'Voodoo') is among the most distinctive in the Blue Note catalogue. Session gravity is high: Tommy Turrentine, Charlie Rouse, Butch Warren and Billy Higgins, with Ike Quebec's celebrated cameo on the ballad 'Deep in a Dream' (S2). The Warren-Higgins rhythm section is the same one that powered Dexter Gordon's Go (already in the canon), so the lineage ties directly into existing canon records. Cool Struttin' is already in the canon; this is its more mature sibling — the record where Clark's artistry peaked before his death at 31.
consensus: AllMusic 4.5 stars (Nastos, 'definitive recording for Clark, and really for all time in the mainstream jazz idiom'); Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings 3.5 stars (Cook & Morton 2008, p.254); The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 3 stars (Swenson 1985, p.41); All About Jazz ('one of his final recordings before an untimely death, everything seemed to solidify with this 1961 ringer').

personnel_record.notes: Single session, November 13, 1961, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ (S1 recording date/location; S2 infobox). Released May 1962 on Blue Note BLP 4091 (mono) / BST 84091 (stereo); conventionally dated by the 1961 recording. Producer Alfred Lion (S2, S3). Engineer Rudy Van Gelder is marked inf: no consulted source names a recording engineer, but the session was cut in Van Gelder's own Englewood Cliffs studio, where he engineered all Blue Note dates (the sanctioned Van Gelder inference). Original six-track LP personnel is fully documented (obs): Turrentine and Rouse are absent on 'Deep in a Dream', which features Ike Quebec's tenor cameo (S1, S2). The 2008 RVG CD reissue adds two bonus tracks from the same session — 'Zellmar's Delight' and 'Melody for C (alternate take)' — whose per-track personnel is not separately documented in the sources consulted, so those two are marked inf (same-session inference) and track_assignments_complete is set false for that reason alone. Track durations follow Wikipedia/AllMusic (S1, S2); Discogs prints marginally different vinyl-label timings (S3). AllMusic styles: Hard Bop, Jazz Instrument, Piano Jazz (S1).

ballot.case_for: Clark's final album as leader before his death at 31 is widely cited as his mature peak — AllMusic's Nastos calls it 'a definitive recording for Clark, and really for all time in the mainstream jazz idiom' (4.5 stars), backed by Penguin Guide 3.5 stars (Cook & Morton 2008) and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide's 3 stars — giving genuine cross-tradition consensus. He wrote four of the six originals, and the hard-bop quintet writing ('Somethin' Special,' 'Voodoo') is among the most distinctive in the Blue Note catalogue. Session gravity is the clincher: Butch Warren and Billy Higgins are the same rhythm section powering Dexter Gordon's Go (already in the canon), Charlie Rouse bridges hard-bop Blue Note to the Monk years ahead, and Ike Quebec's tenor cameo on 'Deep in a Dream' is a historically rich ballad performance from Quebec's own late-period stretch. It still plays as a model of what the hard-bop apex sounded like.
ballot.case_against: The consensus ceiling is real: Penguin's 3.5 is solid but not Crown/Core Collection, the Rolling Stone 3 stars is modest, and no NPR Jazz canon list, DownBeat critics'-poll reference, or label-anthology framing appears in the dossier. Cool Struttin' (1958) is already in the canon and is the album most listeners and critics name first when naming Clark — Leapin' and Lopin' is widely the second Clark, and the defining-statement signal weakens once the load-bearing Clark slot is filled. As lineage it is a culmination of the 1961 hard-bop formula rather than a catalyst that changed what came after — it executes the idiom beautifully without pushing the language forward. Session gravity is solid but not top-tier: Turrentine and a pre-Monk Rouse are excellent sidemen, not the era's defining anchors.
ballot.disagreement: The references split on tier: one argued consensus_core, reading the album as an overwhelming success as a definitive hard-bop statement with immense session gravity; the other argued contested, citing the Penguin 3.5-not-Crown ceiling, the Cool Struttin' shadow capping the defining-statement argument, and session gravity that is solid rather than stellar. Both agreed on priority: strong.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John admit Leapin' and Lopin' as a strong second Sonny Clark — it earns its place on session gravity, compositional maturity, and cross-tradition consensus — but rule on whether that consensus clears the bar for consensus_core or whether the Cool Struttin' shadow and 3.5-not-Crown ceiling keep it contested.
